title: Agentic Finance for Supervisors
summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to understand and supervise AI agents that transact and make financial decisions, from agent identity to payments and liability.
intro: This training programme equips supervisory staff to understand and supervise AI agents that transact and make financial decisions autonomously, from agent identity and delegated authority to payments, market integrity, financial crime and liability.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give supervisors a clear understanding of how AI agents are beginning to act for firms and consumers, and how existing supervisory frameworks apply when software, not people, initiates transactions and decisions. Participants leave able to challenge firms on agent governance, identity, authority and controls, identify red flags and contribute to the authority's policy response.
sections.What It Covers: AI agents and levels of autonomy, the four-layer architecture of agentic finance, use cases and market structure, know your agent and trust frameworks, governance of autonomous decisions, agent-initiated payments and settlement, agents in markets, resilience and security, financial crime, conduct and liability, and supervisory strategy and policy.
Intended Audience: Supervisors of banks, payment and e-money firms, investment firms and crypto-asset service providers adopting AI agents
Policy, innovation, payments and financial crime specialists assessing agent-driven business models
Senior managers shaping the authority's response to AI and autonomous finance
Learning Objectives: Explain how AI agents work, what makes them different from earlier automation and where they are entering finance
Analyse agentic finance through its governance, decision, asset and settlement layers
Assess how firms establish agent identity, delegated authority and trust
Evaluate governance, resilience and market integrity risks where agents act with limited human intervention
Identify financial crime, consumer protection and liability issues in agent-initiated transactions
Design a supervisory and policy response to agentic finance, drawing on FSB and other international work
sections.Structure and Format: Ten modules of about three hours each, grouped into four pathways and delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a multi-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a briefing with scenario exercises, red flags and supervisory questions, and pathways or individual modules can be selected or tailored to the authority's needs.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some understanding of AI in financial services, for example from AI Governance for Supervisors, is helpful. No technical background is required.
Core Reading: FSB, The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence (2024)
OECD, Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence (2019, revised 2024)
NIST, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) (2023)

modules.title: From Automation to Agency: AI Agents in Finance
modules.summary: What AI agents are, how they plan, use tools and act on goals, and why delegating decisions and transactions to software changes the supervisory picture.
objectives: Explain how AI agents combine models, tools, memory and goals
Distinguish agents from rules-based automation, algorithms and chatbots
Identify the levels of autonomy at which agents operate
syllabus: Large language models, tool use and autonomous task execution
Levels of autonomy: assistive, supervised and fully delegated agents
Single-agent and multi-agent systems and agent-to-agent interaction
Capabilities, limits and failure modes: hallucination, goal drift and overreach

modules.title: The Architecture of the Agentic Era
modules.summary: A four-layer model of agentic finance, covering governance, decision, asset and settlement layers, and how it helps supervisors locate risk, control and accountability.
objectives: Explain the governance, decision, asset and settlement layers of agentic finance
Analyse how risk and control points shift between the layers
Map existing regulatory requirements onto each layer
syllabus: Governance layer: mandates, permissions, policies and oversight
Decision layer: models, reasoning and recommendations
Asset layer: accounts, wallets, tokenised assets and custody
Settlement layer: payment rails, stablecoins and programmable money

modules.title: Use Cases and Changing Market Structure
modules.summary: Where agents are already appearing in financial services, from agent-led shopping and treasury to trading and personal finance, and the new intermediaries and dependencies this creates.
objectives: Identify current and emerging agentic use cases across sectors
Analyse the business models of agent providers, platforms and incumbent firms
Evaluate how agents could change competition, distribution and concentration
syllabus: Agentic commerce and consumer-facing financial agents
Corporate treasury, operations and back-office agents
Agents in trading, investment and personal financial management
New intermediaries: agent platforms, tool providers and agent marketplaces

modules.title: Know Your Agent: Identity, Authority and Trust
modules.summary: How firms verify which agent they are dealing with, whom it acts for and what it is allowed to do, and the trust frameworks emerging to make agent identity and delegated authority verifiable.
objectives: Explain the know your agent concept and how it extends customer due diligence
Assess how firms verify agent identity, principal and scope of authority
Evaluate emerging trust frameworks, credentials and registries for agents
syllabus: Binding agents to principals: verifiable credentials and digital identity
Delegated authority: mandates, spending limits, scopes and revocation
Trust frameworks, agent registries and interoperability standards
Red flags: anonymous agents, unbounded mandates and impersonation

modules.title: Governing Autonomous Decision-Making in Firms
modules.summary: What sound governance looks like when agents make or execute decisions for a firm or its customers, and how supervisors test accountability, human oversight and control in practice.
objectives: Assess accountability for agent decisions at board and senior management level
Evaluate guardrails, human oversight and escalation arrangements
Apply model risk and testing expectations to agentic systems
syllabus: Senior manager accountability and agent inventories
Human-in-the-loop, human-on-the-loop and meaningful oversight
Guardrails, permissions, audit trails and kill-switches
Pre-deployment testing, red-teaming and ongoing monitoring

modules.title: Payments and Settlement by Agents
modules.summary: How agents initiate and settle payments across card, account-to-account, tokenised and stablecoin rails, and what this means for authentication, consent, fraud and liability allocation.
objectives: Explain how agent-initiated payments work across traditional and tokenised rails
Assess consent, authentication and authorisation where no human acts at the point of payment
Evaluate how liability for unauthorised or erroneous agent payments is allocated
syllabus: Agent-initiated payments: tokenised credentials, mandates and payment APIs
Strong authentication and consent in delegated transactions
Stablecoins, tokenised deposits and programmable settlement for agents
Disputes, refunds and liability between consumer, agent provider and firm

modules.title: Agents in Markets: Trading, Advice and Market Integrity
modules.summary: The market integrity and conduct risks when agents trade, allocate portfolios and advise or act for clients, including herding, collusion, manipulation and suitability.
objectives: Analyse how agents could amplify herding, volatility and correlated behaviour
Identify risks of emergent collusion and manipulation between agents
Assess suitability and best interest obligations where agents act for clients
syllabus: Agent-driven trading, execution and portfolio management
Herding, flash events and procyclicality from similar models
Algorithmic collusion and agent-driven manipulation
Suitability, best execution and conflicts in agent-mediated advice

modules.title: Resilience, Security and Third-Party Risk in Agentic Systems
modules.summary: How agentic systems can fail or be attacked, how failures cascade across connected agents, and how dependence on a few model and platform providers concentrates risk.
objectives: Identify attack vectors specific to agents, including prompt injection and tool misuse
Assess cascading failure and contagion risk in multi-agent systems
Evaluate concentration, outsourcing and exit risk on model and agent providers
syllabus: Prompt injection, credential theft and compromised tools
Cascading failures and runaway agents: containment and recovery
Third-party and foundation model concentration risk
Incident reporting, resilience testing and the supervisory evidence to request

modules.title: Financial Crime, Conduct and Liability
modules.summary: How agents can be exploited for fraud, money laundering and sanctions evasion, how consumer protection applies when agents act for customers, and who is accountable when things go wrong.
objectives: Identify financial crime typologies that exploit autonomous agents
Assess customer due diligence, monitoring and sanctions controls for agent activity
Evaluate consumer protection and liability where agents act for customers
syllabus: Agent-enabled fraud, synthetic identities and scams at scale
Money laundering and sanctions evasion through agent networks and crypto rails
Fair treatment, vulnerable customers and manipulation of consumer agents
Liability chains: principal, agent provider, platform and regulated firm

modules.title: Supervising the Agentic Era: Strategy and Policy
modules.summary: Brings the programme together into the authority's strategic response, covering international work on AI, perimeter and liability policy, supervisory tools and the authority's own use of agents.
objectives: Compare international approaches to AI and agentic finance, including FSB work
Evaluate perimeter, liability and trust framework policy options
Design a supervisory roadmap for agentic finance
syllabus: International work: FSB, IOSCO, BIS, CPMI, FATF and OECD
Perimeter questions: when an agent provider becomes a regulated activity
Sandboxes, industry engagement and supervisory use of agents
Workshop: the authority's agentic finance roadmap

related.title: AI Governance for Supervisors
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to assess firms' AI governance, model and fairness risk, and to shape the authority's approach to AI supervision.

related.title: The EU AI Act and Financial Services (EU Edition)
related.summary: An eight-module programme on the EU AI Act for supervisors and financial firms: risk classification, high-risk credit and insurance uses, provider and deployer duties, supervision and compliance programmes.

related.title: SupTech, Data and Supervisory Analytics
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors and leaders to govern supervisory data, interrogate returns, use analytics to surface risk and build the authority's SupTech capability.

related.title: Applied AI for Supervisory Staff
related.summary: An eight-module hands-on programme helping supervisory staff use generative AI and analytics tools safely and productively in everyday supervisory work.

related.title: Financial Crime Supervision in the Age of AI
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to assess financial crime controls and firms' use of AI in monitoring, screening, fraud and surveillance.

related.title: FinTech Business Models: Understanding and Supervising Innovation
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors and firm compliance teams to understand how FinTech business models make money, grow and fail, and to assess their risks.
